sentences.text: This animal belonged to the sphenosuchian crocodylomorph group and represented an early branch of the lineage found in South Africa. It was a diminutive, slender creature that lived specifically during the Sinemurian stage of the lower Jurassic.
Its scientific name, leptorhynchus, describes the narrow snout, while its limbs were notably long with the rear legs extending slightly further than the front ones.
Unlike modern crocodiles, this creature moved on land as a predator capable of running.
Scientists suggest it hunted in packs similar to wolves but probably spent its life alone.
The original specimen was unearthed in 1988 by James Kitching, who led the Evolutionary Studies Institute at the University of the Witwatersrand, near Barkly East.
The find initially contained a nearly whole skull, jaw, and various body bones, though Kitching and Christopher Gow first thought they were Pedeticosaurus leviseuri.
Jim Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues later re-examined the material in 2002 to name it a new species, noting that only this single species is currently known.
The skull portion of the holotype has since vanished, leaving the remaining bones stored at the Evolutionary Studies Institute.
Researchers Jim Clark and Hans-Dieter Sues formally introduced the genus in 2002, establishing Litargosuchus leptorhynchus as the defining species.
It is placed within the basal clade Sphenosuchidae and accepted as part of the crown archosaur group, although its precise position remains unclear due to limited knowledge of the family tree.
Fossils appear only in the upper Elliot Formation of South Africa, dating from 201.4 to 192.9 million years ago across the Hettangian to Sinemurian periods.
